name: Cardiogen
maker: St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology (V. Khavinson)

overview.headline: A four-amino-acid peptide named for the heart. Rat and guinea-pig data from its inventors' patent; no human study.
overview.lede: Cardiogen is the Khavinson institute's tetrapeptide Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg, patented in the U.S. in 2010 for "restoring myocardium function". The institute's own 2014 review of its clinical results does not mention it. It is not registered as a medicine, or as far as we could find as a supplement, anywhere.

stats.lbl: 24-hour deaths after an induced heart attack, 20 treated versus 20 untreated rats

stats.src: PubMed, patents, institute publications and registries, Oct 2026

mechanism.intro: A short peptide said to protect heart-muscle cells and their energy supply.

parts.name: The bioregulator idea
parts.text: The 2016 computer model places Cardiogen on the DNA sequence "agtc" with "very strong" predicted binding. A docking calculation, not a measurement in heart tissue.

parts.name: What the animal work showed
parts.text: Rats with a tied-off coronary artery had smaller areas of dead muscle and better mitochondrial energy efficiency a day later; isolated guinea-pig hearts regained more blood flow after 30 minutes without oxygen (10.8 versus 8.5 ml/min). A 2009 institute paper found it slowed a transplanted sarcoma in old rats by damaging the tumour's blood vessels.

more.title: More: where the heart data come from
paras: Nearly all of it sits in a patent, written by the applicant and never peer reviewed; several experiments say their results are "in the tables" without printing them.

results.headline: Rodent heart-injury models in a patent, one rat tumour paper, nothing in people.
results.lede: The "heart repair" claims trace to animal experiments the inventors ran two decades ago and published only in patent filings.

stats.lbl: mentions of Cardiogen in the institute's own 2014 review of its clinical results

items.t: Heart explants and isolated heart cells under low oxygen were tested in the patent; results referred to but not printed. Isolated guinea-pig hearts (60 animals) regained more coronary flow after ischaemia.

Rats with a ligated coronary artery: 24-hour mortality 15% versus 45% (20 per group). Rats with induced arrhythmia: fewer deaths. Old rats with M-1 sarcoma: slower tumour growth, more tumour-cell death (Levdik and Knyazkin 2009). Toxicity tests in 66 mice, 60 rats and 96 guinea pigs: none reported.
None found. The 2014 clinical review covers Thymalin and Epithalamin only; the 2020 monograph lists Cardiogen in a table without data.

more.title: More: why rodent heart models are not a forecast
paras: Countless agents that shrink infarcts in rats have failed in people, and these experiments were small, run by the patent holders and never replicated. The sarcoma finding means Cardiogen altered a tumour's blood supply, a reason for caution until someone understands how.

effects.headline: No human safety data. The only toxicity testing is in the inventors' patent.
effects.lede: Nobody has given Cardiogen to people in a study. The patent reports no rodent toxicity, with a rise in guinea-pig white-cell counts at 3 and 6 months the authors did not treat as harmful.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: Not measurable: no trial has been run and no human report exists.

unique.title: What is actually known
unique.text: Nothing beyond the absence of data. A peptide marketed for the heart has never had its effect on human heart rhythm, blood pressure or cardiac enzymes measured.

more.title: More: what a trial would monitor for
paras: Heart rhythm and blood pressure (the patent reports rhythm effects in rats); blood-vessel and tumour effects (the 2009 sarcoma finding); immune reactions.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: In rodents: fewer early deaths after an induced heart attack, smaller infarcts. In people: nothing measured.

urgent.title: Symptoms a doctor should see promptly
items: Spreading redness, swelling or pus at an injection site, or fever and chills after an injection
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
New palpitations, breathlessness or ankle swelling
urgent.note: No trial has defined this peptide's own danger signs; these relate to an unverified product.

levels.nopk: No one has measured Cardiogen in a person's blood; no half-life or absorption figure exists for it in any species. There is nothing to build a curve from.

stats.src: PubMed, patents, institute publications and registries, Oct 2026

explain.t: The simulator on other pages needs a measured half-life; none exists for Cardiogen.

explain.b: Why the oral claim is contested.
explain.t: Pharmacologists expect peptides this short to be digested by gut and blood enzymes; the institute says they are absorbed intact. Nothing in people settles it.

more.title: More: what this page cannot tell you
paras: What is in a product sold as Cardiogen, or what repeated use does: no independent analysis exists, and no study has followed anyone beyond a few weeks.

trials.headline: No clinical trial, registered or unregistered, could be found.
trials.lede: Even within this family Cardiogen stands out: no Russian clinical report of any size. Its evidence is preclinical and mostly unpublished outside a patent.

more.title: More: how the existing studies were run
paras: Rats and guinea pigs were given the peptide before or after an induced heart injury and compared with untreated animals; old rats carrying a transplanted tumour were treated for ten days. None of this says anything about a person.

running.title: No registered trials
items: No clinical trial of Cardiogen on ClinicalTrials.gov or any registry we could find (October 2026).
No Russian clinical report, controlled or uncontrolled, in the institute's reviews or PubMed.

find.text: Search the registry for "Cardiogen" and its sequence "AEDR". We found no registered trial.

items.label: Canada
items.text: Never authorised by Health Canada as a medicine or natural health product (October 2026).

items.label: United States
items.text: Not FDA-approved; absent from FDA's 503A compounding category list of 14 May 2026.

items.label: Russia
items.text: Not a registered medicine; not among the institute's six licensed products, and no Russian registration of any kind found.

cards.title: What a "bioregulator" claim rests on
cards.text: The claim is that a peptide copied from an organ extract reaches that organ and switches on its genes. For Cardiogen the support is:
items: Computer docking models, test-tube DNA work and cell cultures from one institute; no study has tracked one of these peptides into a human organ.

cards.title: What "research use only" means
cards.text: A "research use only" label is a legal device, not a safety rating. No regulator in Canada or the U.S. has checked what is in a vial sold as Cardiogen, and no toxicology or purity data have been filed in the West.
items: Unlike Pinealon or Bronchogen, Cardiogen is not even registered as a food supplement in Russia as far as we could find.

cards.title: Symptoms to take to a doctor
cards.text: If any of these appear after using such a product, see a doctor and bring the product:
items: Fever, chills, or a hot, swollen injection site
Hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine
New palpitations, breathlessness or ankle swelling
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: the Khavinson peptide family
paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946–2024) directed the St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, which made animal-organ extracts from the 1970s and then designed two- to four-amino-acid peptides from each extract's amino-acid make-up, naming them after target organs. Six products became licensed medicines in the USSR or Russia: Thymalin (1982), Thymogen and Epithalamin (1990), Prostatilen (1992), Cortexin and Retinalamin (1999). The synthetic organ-named peptides sold online are not among them, and none appears in an international trial registry.
